extracted.intended_audience: writers, students of rhetoric, and readers of classical stylistics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from Demetrius on identifying bad (frigid) diction and cultivating graceful/elegant style in prose and poetry, covering causes of frigidity, acceptable exceptions, and many concrete devices that produce charm. Useful for composing and evaluating polished literary or rhetorical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frigidity of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity_of diction may, therefore, arise in four ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demetrius lists four origins: (1) "strange terms"; (2) "epithets" (e.g. 'moist sweat'); (3) "composites"—pompous compounded words (e.g. 'desert-wandering'); (4) "metaphors" used extravagantly (e.g. 'a crisis pale and trembling'). Frigid diction is 'extravagant and impossible' and produces cold, unpleasing wording. Examples and citations given from Homer, Alcidamas, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frigid composition (lack of rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is frigid when it lacks good rhythm, or lacks all rhythm, having long syllables from beginning to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unbroken succession of long syllables makes prose 'highly questionable and entirely lacking in prose rhythm' (example: 'This land, our land, which I now reach, which I find all upstirred.'). Conversely, piled long syllables can be effective in poetry (Tennyson, Shakespeare). Avoid metrical phrases introduced in close succession in prose—this is a mark of frigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate elevated style for trivial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A heightened style used in connexion with a trivial subject recalls the 'ornamented pestle' proverb; magnifying trifles with pomp is frigid and inapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fitness must be observed: 'the style must be appropriate—subdued for humble topics, lofty for high themes.' Exceptions exist (e.g. Polycrates jesting), but generally avoid grand language for little things unless intentionally ironic or playful. One may magnify small things for a rhetorical purpose, but it must be fitting and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and classification of hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: The most frigid of all figures is hyperbole, which is of three kinds: likeness, superiority, and impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole 'transcends the possible' and tends toward frigidity because it suggests the impossible (e.g. 'whiter than snow', 'a match for the winds in speed', 'with her head she has smitten the sky'). Comic poets use hyperbole to produce laughter (e.g. 'they voided entire plains'). Hyperbole can charm (Sappho) if handled deftly; beware impossible claims that read as cold or absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable magnification of small matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Small things may be magnified in a way that is not unbecoming and may be necessary to make a point (e.g. to justify punitive seriousness for a small offense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorically justify the magnification: show how small transgressions lead to larger ones, invoke proverbs ('the thin end of the wedge'), or otherwise argue why solemn treatment is warranted. The device is permissible when the magnification serves a reasoned rhetorical purpose rather than mere pomp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding imposture and inflated claims in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposture in style resembles frigidity: boasting or investing trifles with pomp that do not belong to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't attribute qualities to subject or speaker that are not supported by content. Inflated language that pretends greatness where there is none is inartistic; strive for honesty and appropriate magnitude of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace from compression (brevity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The very first grace of style is that which comes from compression: a thought spoiled by dwelling on it is made graceful by a rapid touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise clinching phrases ('and so it was') to achieve charm. Avoid overdevelopment of a simple point; sometimes a brief, decisive phrase produces elegance and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace from conveying multiple ideas succinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: The conveyance of two ideas in one sentence often has a graceful effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Packing related facts or customs into a single compact expression (example: 'Her bow lay strung, her quiver full, her buckler by her head; their girdles they never loose.') yields elegance through concision and economy of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace from arrangement (placement for effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement: a thought often gains charm when placed at the end of a sentence rather than at the beginning or middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the novel, unusual, or climactic element at the sentence end to produce surprise and emphasis (example: listing customary presents first, ending with 'the assurance that his country should be no longer plundered'). Reorder clauses to maximize charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace from rhetorical figures and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures such as redoubling (repetition), anaphora, and similar devices produce grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sappho's redoubling ('Maidenhood, Maidenhood...') and anaphora ('thou bringest...') produce charm by repeated phrasing. Use repetition to reinforce feeling or rhythm, but avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm from choice of words, metaphor, and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of apt epithets, metaphor, and vivid imagery can embellish and give charm to otherwise plain subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epithets like 'wan-brown' and metaphors (nightingale imagery, cicala passage) add delight. Imagery should be relevant and tasteful; the theme may also itself possess inherent grace that diction can enhance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm from coined words and unusual diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Coined words, novel compounds, and even pedestrian terms used freshly can be sources of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: turning 'sole' into 'solitary' or using a pedestrian word in a fresh context yields charm. Dithyrambic compounds suit comic and satyric poetry; use inventive vocabulary sparingly and appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm from recantation, veiled meaning, and allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices like recantation (taking back a phrase), veiled or dark sayings, and allusive reference to other writers increase charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sappho's recanting enhances passion; veiled meanings and ironic references (mocking Homer or other poets) can add wit and subtlety. Such devices may be coarse if used crudely (e.g. ugly jests suited to lower drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit from the unexpected and absence of sequence (griphus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sort of wit arises from the unexpected or from lack of connection with what precedes (griphus), producing startling pleasantries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cyclops' 'Noman' jest, Boulias' incoherent speech, and other startling turns. Use want of sequence deliberately for comic or surprising effect; ensure it suits genre and tone (comic poets exploit this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit from parallelism and similarity of sentence members
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity or parallelism of sentence members often produces a witty effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I went from Athens to Stageira because of the great king, and from Stageira to Athens because of the great storm.' Parallel endings accentuate irony or wit. Employ balanced structures to create rhetorical punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic and prose effects (accumulated long syllables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulated long syllables and metrical phrasing can be frigid in prose but effective and expressive in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing metrical phrases consecutively in prose where they create a monotonous or pompous tone. In poetry, authors (e.g., Tennyson, Shakespeare, Catullus) can make expressive use of accumulated long syllables; choose medium accordingly.
